{{Short description|Proposition in complex analysis}}
{{No footnotes|date=March 2025}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[complex analysis]], '''Osgood's lemma''' states that a [[continuous function]] of several [[complex variable]]s that is [[holomorphic function|holomorphic]] in each variable separately is itself holomorphic. It was introduced by [[William Fogg Osgood]] in 1899.{{sfnp|Osgood|1899}} 

The assumption that the function is continuous can be dropped, but that form of the lemma is much harder to prove and is known as [[Hartogs' theorem]].

There is no analogue of this result for real variables. If it is assumed that a function <math>f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}</math> is globally continuous and separately differentiable on each variable (all partial derivatives exist everywhere), it is not true that <math>f</math> will necessarily be differentiable. A counterexample in two dimensions is given by
:<math>f(x,y)=\dfrac{2x^2y+y^3}{x^2+y^2}.</math>
If in addition it is defined that <math>f(0,0)=0</math>, this function is everywhere continuous and has well-defined partial derivatives in <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> everywhere (also at the origin), but is not differentiable at the origin.
